title: The Copper Bridge
premise: In 1916, field nurse Freya Pemberton secretly records the names of wounded soldiers the officers' reports omit, believing every life deserves a witness. When a stranger named Elias Thorn arrives at her hospital carrying a letter in handwriting that matches a soldier officially listed as dead, Freya discovers her ledger may be the only proof that a man declared an enemy deserter is alive, imprisoned, and awaiting execution. Bound by a promise made in peacetime to his mother, Freya and Elias forge papers, bribe clerks, and cross occupied territory to reach him before the sentence is carried out. The rescue succeeds at terrible cost — Elias dies covering their escape — and Freya returns home to publish the ledger under a false name, finally claiming her own identity as the woman who refused to let the war erase anyone.
about_author: Coral Villalobos is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unsent letters from the First World War before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted ferry house on the coast, where she keeps a wall of names she refuses to forget.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Mattress
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In a crowded field hospital near Ypres, Freya tends the wounded by day and records forgotten names by night, hiding her ledger beneath her cot. A matron nearly catches her. The beat establishes her quiet defiance and the loneliness of being the only one who counts the uncounted.

chapters.title: Names That Fit Nowhere
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A dying private begs her to write to a sister whose address he can't recall; another soldier has no name at all. Freya invents a system of coded entries. The emotional beat is grief sharpened into purpose — she will not let paperwork decide who mattered.

chapters.title: The Stranger at the Gate
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Elias Thorn arrives during a bombardment, mud-caked and half-mad, clutching a letter he won't surrender to officers. He asks for Nurse Pemberton by name. The chapter ends on suspicion: how did he know her, and why does the handwriting on his letter look like a dead man's?

chapters.title: Handwriting of a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. In the laundry tent, Elias shows Freya the letter — from Tomas Reyes, officially killed at Verdun, whom both knew in peacetime. The ink is fresh. Freya's hands shake as she compares it to letters she once filed. Beat: disbelief curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What the Officers Filed Away
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya searches the casualty records and finds Tomas listed as dead — then finds a second entry, redacted, marking him 'transferred, enemy jurisdiction.' Someone knows he's alive. Beat: the first taste of institutional menace.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Flashback to 1913: a garden party where Tomas's mother, Doña Inés, made Elias and Freya swear that if war ever came, they would look after her son. Elias confesses he failed once already. Beat: guilt as fuel; the promise becomes binding again.

chapters.title: The Matron's Price
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Matron Halloway catches Freya copying records — but instead of reporting her, offers silence in exchange for a favor: smuggle medicine to a contact behind the lines. Alliances form out of mutual leverage. Beat: uneasy trust.

chapters.title: Enemy Jurisdiction
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Through a bribed clerk, they learn Tomas was captured wearing civilian clothes and condemned as a spy, held at a fortress prison at Saint-Aubin with execution set for six weeks hence. Beat: the clock starts ticking; the abstract promise becomes a deadline.

chapters.title: Forging the Living
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya uses her ledger knowledge of real soldiers' details to forge travel passes for herself and Elias. The irony stings: she who hated falsified records now falsifies them to save a life. Beat: moral compromise accepted without apology.

chapters.title: Departure Without Leave
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. They slip out of the hospital sector during a supply convoy, leaving Freya's post and reputation behind. A checkpoint nearly exposes them. Beat: point of no return — there is no going back to the people they were yesterday.

chapters.title: Roads Full of Rumor
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. On refugee-choked roads, they hear contradictory stories about Saint-Aubin: some say the executions are postponed, some say accelerated. Freya begins keeping a new ledger — of everyone they meet who helps them. Beat: kindness found in wreckage.

chapters.title: The Ferryman's Debt
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. A river crossing hinges on an old boatman who once owed Tomas's father money. He takes them but warns that informers watch every bridge. Beat: gratitude shadowed by paranoia; nowhere is neutral anymore.

chapters.title: A Face From the Hospital
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In a market town, Freya recognizes Sergeant Doyle, a gossiping orderly from her unit. She lies brilliantly about their errand — then realizes he didn't believe a word. Beat: the noose of exposure tightening.

chapters.title: What Elias Carried Home in 1914
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias reveals why he vanished after the war began: he deserted his own commission rather than fire on men he'd grown up beside, including Tomas. His identity is itself a crime. Beat: vulnerability exchanged for trust between the two travelers.

chapters.title: The Convent at Marlenne
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Nuns shelter them for two nights; an old abbess reads Freya's forged papers and quietly corrects her Latin. Freya confesses the whole plan. Beat: absolution without judgment — someone finally sees all of her and stays.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The abbess gives them a bundle of undelivered letters, among them one from Doña Inés to Tomas, written months ago. Reading it aloud, Elias breaks down. Beat: grief transformed into resolve; they carry her words like a weapon.

chapters.title: Doyle Cashes In
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Word reaches them that Doyle reported two deserters matching their description; patrols thicken on the roads. Their forged names are burned into memory and abandoned. Beat: hunted — the story shifts from stealth to pursuit.

chapters.title: The Copper Bridge Itself
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. They reach the old copper-roofed bridge outside Saint-Aubin, the only crossing not watched — because it's believed mined. Elias tests it alone at night, step by step. Beat: terror rendered physical; the title's symbol becomes literal passage between lives.

chapters.title: Inside the Fortress Walls
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Disguised as Red Cross inspectors, they enter Saint-Aubin's outer compound and see the prison yard, the gallows frame already standing. Beat: horror made concrete; hope and dread occupy the same breath.

chapters.title: Cell Block Nine
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. A sympathetic guard, paid in the abbess's letters' news, lets Elias glimpse Tomas through a grate — alive, thinner, unbroken. Tomas doesn't recognize him at first. Beat: joy colliding with the impossibility of getting him out.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Names
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya learns twenty-two prisoners share Tomas's death warrant, most of them local boys conscripted wrongly. Her ledger instinct ignites: she cannot save one name and abandon twenty-one. Beat: the theme crystallizes — justice outside the law must be justice for all of them.

chapters.title: The Guard Who Counts Too
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The guard, Corporal Vasseur, reveals he keeps his own list of the condemned, unable to act alone. Two ledgers, two strangers, one conspiracy. Beat: solidarity across enemy lines; belonging defined by choice, not nation.

chapters.title: A Plan With No Margin
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The three plot a mass escape timed to a prisoner transfer to the gallows: swapped documents, a cut lock, the copper bridge at dawn. Every piece depends on perfect timing. Beat: tension coiling; the reader sees exactly what can go wrong.

chapters.title: Everything That Can Go Wrong
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The transfer moves up two days. Vasseur is reassigned. A key document goes missing. The plan must be rebuilt overnight from scraps. Beat: despair — and the discovery that improvisation, not perfection, is what courage actually looks like.

chapters.title: Night Before the Gallows
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya sits with Tomas in the infirmary under pretense of a last medical inspection. They speak of gardens, of his mother, of nothing important. Beat: stillness before the storm; love expressed as ordinary conversation.

chapters.title: Dawn Transfer
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The execution convoy forms. Vasseur, having talked his way back onto duty, swaps the manifest. Twenty-two men march toward the bridge instead of the gallows. Beat: the gamble in motion, every second weighted.

chapters.title: The Bridge Holds
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The escapees cross the copper bridge in fog while a sentry's alarm rises behind them. The bridge holds — barely, groaning, one plank giving way beneath the last man. Beat: exaltation edged with panic; the midpoint miracle.

chapters.title: The Cost of Covering Fire
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Pursuers close on the rear of the column. Elias turns back to hold the bridgehead so the others can scatter into the marshes. He is shot as the last prisoner clears the far bank. Beat: sacrifice — the promise kept with his life.

chapters.title: Carrying Him Home
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya and Tomas drag Elias into the marshes; he dies at dawn asking only that his real name be entered somewhere permanent. Freya writes it in the ledger with numb hands. Beat: devastating loss transmuted into witness.

chapters.title: Twenty-One Directions
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV (first use). Tomas leads the scattered fugitives through wetlands using boyhood knowledge of these fields, while Freya organizes safe houses. Beat: role reversal — the rescued becomes rescuer; Freya learns she cannot carry everything alone.

chapters.title: The Net Closes on Saint-Aubin
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Retribution falls on the fortress: Vasseur arrested, the abbess questioned, the convent searched. News arrives that could unravel everything. Beat: guilt and fear — survival purchased with other people's danger.

chapters.title: Vasseur's Silence
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Vasseur, interrogated, says nothing that leads to the escapees; his fate remains unknown. Tomas wrestles with owing his life to a man who may die for it. Beat: the moral weight of borrowed safety.

chapters.title: Doña Inés's Door
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. They reach Doña Inés's house across the border. Mother and son reunite in a doorway, wordless. Freya delivers Elias's message and shows her the ledger with his name entered. Beat: catharsis — the promise fulfilled, grief given a place to rest.

chapters.title: The Question of Going Back
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas urges Freya to stay, safe, anonymous. Freya realizes the ledger back at the front — years of names — is still hidden under her mattress, waiting to be seized or lost. Beat: identity asserted; she chooses the dangerous thing because it is hers.

chapters.title: Return Under a False Flag
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya re-enters the war zone as a Red Cross clerk under a borrowed name, retrieves the ledger from the hospital, and copies it twice, hiding each copy differently. Beat: quiet triumph; the archivist of the uncounted secures her archive.

chapters.title: Publication in Wartime
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Working with a neutral-country printer, Freya prepares the ledger for publication under the pseudonym 'Coral Villalobos' — the pen name becoming part of the story itself. Beat: agency reclaimed; writing as resistance.

chapters.title: The Trial of Corporal Vasseur
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Vasseur stands court-martialled; the published ledger, smuggled widely, creates public pressure that spares his life and forces review of the remaining warrants. Beat: justice achieved sideways — not by law's mercy but by law's embarrassment.

chapters.title: Armistice Morning
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The guns fall silent. Freya walks a road full of weeping strangers and feels neither triumph nor relief, only the weight of every name. She visits the copper bridge, repaired, ordinary, gleaming. Beat: elegy — victory and loss indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Every Name Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. In a village hall, survivors and families gather as Freya, still pseudonymous, reads the ledger aloud — hundreds of names, ending with Elias Thorn's. Doña Inés and Tomas sit in the front row. Beat: communal mourning turned into communal belonging.

chapters.title: The Woman Behind the Name
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Years later, an aging Freya donates the original ledger to an archive, signing the accession card with her true name for the first time. The curator asks if Coral Villalobos was a real person. 'She was everyone the record forgot,' Freya says. Final beat: identity fully claimed — belonging earned, justice witnessed, the promise complete.
